text: 🇲🇽⚖️ "The law is very clear here. Here there was Juárez, here there were liberals. Here there was a civil war over this issue that took away special privileges." — President Claudia Sheinbaum, Mañanera, Oct 21, 2026 Canal 14 asked about a religious association close to a PRI deputy handing awards to PAN and PRI figures inside the Chamber of Deputies, and whether churches could promote candidates in Mexico as they have elsewhere in Latin America. Sheinbaum said the Chamber should not host such events, and the law clearly limits how far all religious organizations and ministers can take part in politics. Juárez's Reform War (1858–61) separated church and state; a 1992 reform restored relations with the Vatican. "That doesn't happen in other Latin American countries because they did not live through these processes."

🇲🇽🛢️ "Today Pemex produces more energy for Mexico and generates more value inside the country." — Juan Carlos Carpio, Pemex CEO, Mañanera, Oct 21, 2026 In under two years Pemex cut its debt by more than $20 billion, to its lowest level since 2014. Its gasoline, diesel and jet fuel output is up 186% from 2018, from 350,000 to 1 million barrels a day. Gasoline and diesel sales rose 17.9% in January–September, and urea output is up 36%. Sheinbaum said the treasury once took as much as 85% from Pemex. It now pays a single 30% production duty, plus income tax, leaving more to invest. "We didn't do this to now put it back in debt up to $100 billion."

🇲🇽🛢️ Fuel smuggling cost 61 billion pesos in unpaid fuel tax in 2025. "What interests us is to eradicate it." — President Claudia Sheinbaum, Mañanera, Oct 21, 2026 16 agencies now share data in a single fuel monitoring center that follows every link of the chain, from importer to gas station. Crossing the invoices found 2025 imbalances worth 61.7 billion pesos, mostly among fuel traders with no physical assets, a figure the government now wants to cut out by law. Through September 2026, an extra 48 billion pesos in fuel excise tax (IEPS) has been recorded. Licensed fuel importers went from 197 to 17. 2,539 people have been arrested, and 5,572 tankers and other vehicles and 173.7 million liters of fuel seized. In the Altamira tanker case, 15 people are detained and 17 arrest warrants are pending, three with extradition requests to the US.

🇲🇽📊 <u>Peso Hits 18.65, an 11-Month Low, as the Middle East War Drags On</u>

The peso fell 1.15% to 18.6395 per dollar on Wednesday morning and touched 18.65, its weakest level in 11 months, El Economista reports. The pressure comes from abroad: Iran says there will be no peace until the naval blockade and oil sanctions are lifted, and the Fed's September rate hike has squeezed the carry trade. Monex says the rate is testing a break of the 18.50 technical level "affected by traders' caution over the geopolitical risk premium from the Middle East." At home, retail sales rose 1.2% in August and 3.2% year on year.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>PRI Leader Karla Ayala Formally Charged Over Salary Kickbacks</u>

Karla Ayala Villalobos, a former PRI federal deputy who now sits on Alito Moreno's national executive committee, has been formally charged with abuse of authority. María Fernanda Moreno Salas, her former technical secretary on the Chamber of Deputies Youth Commission, says Ayala demanded 13,000 pesos a month out of her salary. She paid for nearly a year out of fear of losing her job, and when she stopped, she lost it.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>Broken Contracts, False Information: Three More Suppliers Banned</u>

Mexico's Anti-Corruption and Good Government Ministry barred AM Cenit, Construcciones Zárate Prados and Ezequiel Becerril Barrera from public contracts and fined them a combined 2,108,852 pesos. AM Cenit took the biggest hit, a 1,346,268-peso fine and a 15-month ban, after two of its contracts, with the federal prison system and with Profepa, were rescinded. Becerril was caught giving false information in a Health Ministry tender.

🇲🇽🌎 <u>Mexico at the UN: We Reject the Committee's Reading of Article 34</u>

At the UN General Assembly's Third Committee, Interior Ministry undersecretary Arturo Medina Padilla rejected the Committee on Enforced Disappearances' interpretation of Article 34, the clause it activated against Mexico in March. The committee itself found no evidence of a federal policy of disappearances. Medina Padilla cited more than 16,000 people located in 2026, a review of the national registry alongside the UN human rights office, and forensic cooperation with Germany, Spain, Norway, Canada and Guatemala. "Our commitment is clear: find the disappeared, fight impunity and guarantee the rights of families."

🇲🇽🏥 <u>IMSS Raises Its Pay Offer to 8% and Makes 10,939 Jobs Permanent</u>

IMSS's Technical Council approved an 8% raise for its workers, up from the 6.8% offer they rejected in the wage consultation. Director Zoé Robledo said 4% goes straight into base salary and 4% into housing assistance. The package also gives permanent positions to 10,939 workers, including staff hired during Covid, plus more medicine, equipment and hospital maintenance. Sheinbaum had said the money would come from cutting administrative spending.

🇲🇽💧 <u>Federal Money for Guadalajara's Clean Water: Up to 13 Billion Pesos</u>

President Sheinbaum announced that the federal government will fund a water treatment plant for metropolitan Guadalajara. Conagua director Efraín Morales puts the cost at 12 to 13 billion pesos. Jalisco is already building its own plant worth about 7.5 billion. Federal and state teams meet today to settle the financing, with the goal of doing it without new debt. Ten days ago, thousands marched in Guadalajara over dirty tap water.

🇲🇽📊 <u>Hacienda Pushes 238 Billion Pesos of Debt Out to 2047</u>

Mexico's Finance Ministry refinanced 238.153 billion pesos of domestic debt, swapping Cetes, Bondes F, Bonos M and Udibonos maturing between 2026 and 2043 for paper running to 2047 and stretching the average maturity by 2.9 years, El Economista reports. 123.9 billion of it was due in 2027. It is the sixth operation of the year: debt service came in 121.9 billion pesos under budget in January-August, and the broadest measure of public debt sits at 51.5% of GDP, mostly in pesos at fixed rates.
